Conversation content on Day 53: [|User|]: Here is a piece of text: Dr. Andrew Baker walks a fine line between hope and reality.
Baker is the critical care chief at St. Michael’s Hospital. He is an intensivist, a medical specialist trained in the care of gravely ill patients, typically in intensive-care wards. And that responsibility includes helping those individuals and their families manage the constellations of emotions that accompany the process of death and dying.
Baker talks to families who are coming to grips with losing a loved one about three times a week. He calls these difficult conversations “clarity meetings” at which he tries to reach accord on the next steps in care.
He uses a formula of empathy and sincerity to peel back the layers and help people realize that. That means taking the time to be with them.
And that includes understanding the feelings that surround death.
The intensivist manages a daunting workload, overseeing intensive care and trauma beds, a neurotrauma research lab, graduate students and formidable administrative duties. He is an international expert on time of death.
He lives with his second wife and four blended children, two from each side. He’s lost both his mother and father, and when he encounters a family in the midst of tragedy he sees the people he has loved and lost.
He’s learned to be present in each moment. That’s his formula for happiness.
“When I see my children, I love that moment,” he says. “I like all the little moments, very little moments. Life is about inherent dignity, hope and enjoying the moment.
Baker’s favourite form of relaxation is the sailboat his family keeps docked at the Toronto Islands. “There’s nothing more beautiful than taking out the sailboat, turning off the engine and just having the sails up,” he says.
“It’s incumbent on all of us as we journey through life to come to some sort of graceful understanding of our own mortality,” he says.
So while he walks people through their most painful experiences, he sees them as reminders that life is beautiful. The work has shaped the man, who in turn comforts these loving groups of people we know as families.

Based on the text material above, generate the response to the following quesion or instruction: How has Dr. Andrew Baker's work as an intensivist shaped him as a person?
[|AI|]: Dr. Andrew Baker's work as an intensivist has shaped him as a person by helping him to be present in each moment and to understand the importance of enjoying the little moments in life. He has also learned to be empathetic and sincere in his interactions with families who are facing loss and to help them manage the emotions that come with death and dying. Baker's work has reminded him that life is beautiful, even in the midst of tragedy, and has taught him to come to a graceful understanding of his own mortality.

- Never Have Your Dog Stuffed: "I listened to this on audiobook through the public library. I was anticipating that this would be narrated by the author. Unfortunately, my copy was not. Listening to Mr. Alda tell his story would have made this a 5-star review for me. Nonetheless, it was an enjoyable listening experience. This memoir starts in childhood, growing up with his actor father Robert Alda and his mentally ill mother and his early experience in burlesque houses. He talks about his education and stint in the military. He writes about his struggles to break into acting working on stage, in movies, and on television. He marries and has three daughters. Of course, he writes about his decision to be on M*A*S*H* and some film work after that. He writes excitedly about his time hosting Scientific American Frontiers. He talks about his desire to write and direct and about how he learned to be an actor. If you are looking for a gossipy Hollywood memoir, you are looking at the wrong book. Any mention of other actors is kind and sweetly funny. As other reviewers have mentioned, in listening to this book, you feel like you are sitting down with Mr. Alda for a long chat. His humor, intelligence, energy, and natural curiosity shine through. I am glad that I was able to learn about."
